steps.title: Import React and all hooks needed for this lesson (useState, useEffect)
steps.instruction: Import React, useState, and useEffect from 'react'.
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in the necessary modules. The syntax is: import { React, useState, useEffect } from 'react';
steps.analogousExample:
// Importing modules for a different component
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.seedCode: // Import React, useState, and useEffect here
steps.expectedOutcome: The import statement for React, useState, and useEffect is added to the file.
successCriteria: React, useState, and useEffect are imported from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported React, useState, and useEffect. These are essential for building the useFetch custom hook.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've imported some of the required modules. Make sure to import React, useState, and useEffect from 'react'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The import statement is missing or incorrect. You need to import React, useState, and useEffect from 'react'.

steps.title: Create the useFetch custom hook function
steps.instruction: Create a function called 'useFetch' that takes a 'url' parameter. The function should return nothing for now (just an empty body).
steps.hint: You can use either a function declaration or arrow function syntax. Remember to include the url parameter in parentheses.
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState, useEffect } from 'react';

// Create your useFetch function here
steps.expectedOutcome: A useFetch function with a url parameter is defined in your code.
successCriteria: The useFetch function is created with a url parameter and an empty function body.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the useFetch custom hook function with a url parameter.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you've created a function called 'useFetch' that accepts a 'url' parameter.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function wasn't created correctly. Check that you've named it 'useFetch' and included a 'url' parameter.

steps.title: Initialize state variables for data, loading, and error
steps.instruction: Inside the useFetch function, use useState to create three state variables: 'data' (initialized to null), 'loading' (initialized to true), and 'error' (initialized to null).
steps.hint: Call useState three times with appropriate initial values. For example: const [data, setData] = useState(null);
steps.expectedOutcome: The useFetch function will have three state variables ready to track fetched data, loading status, and errors.
successCriteria: The useFetch function contains three useState calls with variables named data (initial null), loading (initial true), and error (initial null).
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully set up the state variables needed to track the API response.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created some state variables, but make sure you have all three: data, loading, and error with the correct initial values.
steps.feedbackWrong: The state variables aren't set up correctly. Check that you're using useState three times with the specified names and initial values.

steps.title: Define the fetchData async function inside useFetch
steps.instruction: Inside your useFetch function, define an async function called fetchData that will handle the API call. The function should be empty for now (just add the function declaration).
steps.hint: Remember to use the 'async' keyword before the function definition. You can place this function anywhere inside the useFetch function body.
steps.expectedOutcome: Your useFetch function now contains an empty async fetchData function declaration.
successCriteria: The useFetch function contains an async function named fetchData defined inside it.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully defined the fetchData async function. This will be the core function that handles the API fetching logic.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've defined an async function named fetchData inside the useFetch function.
steps.feedbackWrong: Please define an async function called fetchData inside the useFetch function. Remember to use the async keyword.

steps.title: Call fetchData inside useEffect
steps.instruction: Add a useEffect hook inside your useFetch function that calls fetchData and has the url as a dependency.
steps.hint: Remember to import useEffect if you haven't already (it's already imported). Inside useEffect, call fetchData(). Make sure to include [url] as the dependency array.
steps.expectedOutcome: The useEffect hook will trigger fetchData whenever the url changes.
successCriteria: useEffect is added inside useFetch, calls fetchData, and has [url] as its dependency array.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've correctly added useEffect to trigger the fetch when the URL changes.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure useEffect calls fetchData and includes [url] in the dependency array.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try again. Remember to add useEffect inside useFetch, call fetchData inside it, and pass [url] as a dependency.

steps.title: Return the state values from useFetch
steps.instruction: Inside the useFetch function, add a return statement at the end that returns an object containing the data, loading, and error state variables.
steps.hint: The return statement should come after the useEffect hook and return an object like { data, loading, error }.
steps.expectedOutcome: The useFetch hook now returns an object with the three state values, making them available to any component that calls the hook.
successCriteria: The useFetch function ends with a return statement that returns an object containing data, loading, and error.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully returned the state values from the useFetch hook, making them accessible to components.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're returning an object with all three state values: data, loading, and error.
steps.feedbackWrong: The useFetch hook should return an object containing the data, loading, and error state variables.

steps.title: Create a main App component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named App that returns a simple wrapper element (like a div).
steps.hint: Define a function called App that returns JSX. You can start by returning an empty div for now.
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component is defined and returns a div wrapper.
successCriteria: A functional component named App is created and returns a div element.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created the App component that will use the useFetch hook.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure the component is named exactly 'App' and returns a div element.
steps.feedbackWrong: The App component isn't defined correctly. Check that you've created a function named App that returns JSX.

steps.title: Use the useFetch hook in App with a sample API URL
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, call the useFetch hook with a sample API URL (like 'https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/todos/1') and destructure its return values into data, loading, and error variables.
steps.hint: Call the useFetch hook inside your App component and destructure the returned object into three variables.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: calling a custom hook and destructuring
const { value, status } = useCustomHook('some-argument');
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component now calls the useFetch hook with a sample URL and has access to the data, loading, and error state values.
successCriteria: useFetch is called with a sample URL string, and its return values are destructured into data, loading, and error variables inside App.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully called the useFetch hook and destructured its return values. Now you have access to the data, loading state, and any error that might occur.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're calling useFetch with a URL string argument and destructuring all three values (data, loading, error).
steps.feedbackWrong: The App component should call the useFetch hook with a sample URL and destructure its return values. Check that you're passing a string URL to useFetch and using object destructuring.

steps.title: Add conditional rendering for loading state
steps.instruction: Inside your App component's return statement, add conditional rendering that shows a loading message when the loading state from useFetch is true.
steps.hint: Use a ternary operator or logical && operator to conditionally render a paragraph element with text like 'Loading...' based on the loading variable.
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component will conditionally display a loading message when data is being fetched.
successCriteria: The App component contains conditional rendering that displays a loading message when the loading state is true.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added conditional rendering for the loading state. The loading message will appear while data is being fetched.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using the loading variable from useFetch in your conditional rendering.
steps.feedbackWrong: The conditional rendering for loading state isn't quite right. Check that you're using the loading variable and displaying a message when it's true.

steps.title: Add conditional rendering for error and data states
steps.instruction: In your App component's JSX, after the loading conditional, add a ternary operator that shows an error message if error exists, otherwise displays the fetched data.
steps.hint:
You can use the destructured error and data variables from useFetch. The structure would be: error ?

Error message

:

Data content

.
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component will now display an error message when there's an error, or show the fetched data when successful.
successCriteria: The JSX includes a ternary operator that conditionally renders an error message or the data based on the error state.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully implemented conditional rendering for both error and data states, completing the useFetch lesson.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using a ternary operator with error and data from useFetch.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check the instruction: you need to add a ternary operator that shows an error message if error exists, otherwise displays the data.
